name: Abbasid Caliphate
summary: The caliphate of the Islamic Golden Age, centred on Baghdad and the House of Wisdom, until the Mongol sack of 1258.

knownFor.label: House of Wisdom
knownFor.note: A Baghdad centre for translation and science.

knownFor.label: Paper mills
knownFor.note: Baghdad’s paper mill spread papermaking west.

knownFor.label: Algebra (al-Khwarizmi)
knownFor.note: The word “algorithm” comes from his name.

knownFor.label: Thousand and One Nights
knownFor.note: Stories set at the court of Harun al-Rashid.

location.value: Ruled from Iraq, mainly from Baghdad. At first it held most of the former Umayyad lands except Spain, from North Africa to Central Asia.

terrain.value: The Tigris–Euphrates river valleys of Iraq, with Iran, Khurasan, Syria and Egypt as major provinces.

climate.value: Arid to semi-arid. Irrigated agriculture in Iraq.
climate.source: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (3rd ed., 2016)

resources.value: Iraq’s irrigated farmland, trade, and paper production (from the 790s).

disasters.value: Damaging floods, before the Mongol invasion of 1258; plagues are not recorded in the sources checked.

urbanisation.value: Baghdad, founded in 762 as a round city, grew larger than Rome by the 9th century and was one of the world’s greatest cities.

disease.value: Not detailed in the sources checked.

migration.value: A multi-ethnic, multi-religious capital. Persians and other non-Arab Muslims (mawali) entered the elite. Turkic slave-soldiers were brought in from the 830s.

economicBase.value: Agriculture, trade and crafts across a huge single market, plus a large paper industry.

tradeRoutes.value: The Silk Road and Indian Ocean routes linking China, India, the Middle East, Africa and Europe. Samanid lands thrived on trade.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate in the sources checked. Baghdad had grown larger than Rome from the 9th century.

moneyAndTax.value: Gold dinars and silver dirhams. Revenue fell when military land grants (iqta) spread and provinces became autonomous.

inequality.value: A wealthy court and merchant class above peasants and slaves. Large slave-labour uprisings occurred (the Zanj rebellion, 869–883).

governmentType.value: A hereditary monarchy under a caliph, with a vizier and a large bureaucracy. From 945 the caliphs became figureheads under the Buyids, then the Seljuks.

keyRulers.value: Al-Saffah (750–754, founder). Al-Mansur (founded Baghdad, 762). Harun al-Rashid (786–809). Al-Maʿmun (813–833). Al-Nasir (1180–1225, revival). Al-Mustaʿsim (last in Baghdad, killed 1258).
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Abbasid Caliphate (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox); Britannica: Abbasid caliphate (checked 8 Nov 2026)

succession.value: Hereditary in the Abbas family, but disputed: Harun divided the succession between his sons, which led to civil war (the Fourth Fitna, 811–813).

institutions.value: The vizier and bureaucratic ministries, Islamic law schools, the House of Wisdom, and a standing army of Turkic slave-soldiers (from al-Muʿtasim).

stability.value: The Fourth Fitna (811–813). The Anarchy at Samarra (861–870). The Zanj rebellion. Provinces breaking away (Aghlabids, Tulunids, Samanids, Fatimids).

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between court factions, viziers and Turkic military commanders, who made and unmade caliphs in the 860s.

armyAndTech.value: First the Khurasani revolutionary army, then a professional standing army recruited mainly from Turkic slaves.

majorWars.value: The Abbasid revolution and Battle of the Zab (750). The Battle of Talas against Tang China (751). Wars with Byzantium. The Mongol siege and sack of Baghdad (1258).

territoryChange.value: Lost Spain (756), then North Africa and Egypt (to the Fatimids, from 909) and eastern provinces to autonomous dynasties. By the 10th century it controlled little directly.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Byzantium, the Umayyads of Córdoba, the Fatimids, and later the Mongols. Diplomatic contacts with Tang China and Charlemagne.

inventions.value: Paper mills (Baghdad, 794). Advances in algebra (al-Khwarizmi), chemistry (Jabir ibn Hayyan), astronomy, optics and medicine.

scienceEducation.value: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and extended them, the heart of the “Islamic Golden Age”. Later the Mustansiriya madrasa (1227/1234).

openness.value: Highly open: it absorbed Greek, Persian and Indian learning and welcomed Christian, Jewish and Persian scholars.

communicationTransport.value: Silk Road caravan routes crossed the caliphate; Arab merchants dominated Indian Ocean trade; paper mill in Baghdad from 794.

religion.value: Islam was the state religion, with Christian, Jewish and Zoroastrian minorities. Al-Maʿmun’s inquisition (the Mihna, 833–848) tried to impose Muʿtazili theology.

languageWriting.value: Arabic was official and the language of science. Persian revived in the east (Samanids).

artsArchitecture.value: The round city of Baghdad, Samarra’s Great Mosque and spiral minaret, and the One Thousand and One Nights, which took shape around the 10th century.

socialStructure.value: Caliph and court, Arab and Persian elites, ulama (scholars), merchants, peasants, protected non-Muslims, and slaves (including soldiers and labourers).

sharedIdentity.value: A cosmopolitan Islamic identity, less Arab-centred than the Umayyads.

dailyLife.value: Courtyard houses with fountains in Baghdad; bread, rice, dates and spices; public baths and markets.

neighbours.value: The Byzantine Empire, Tang China, Khazars, Turkic peoples, Indian kingdoms, Fatimid Egypt and the Umayyads of Spain.

ideasReligions.value: Transmitted Greek science and Indian numerals (via Arabic works) to medieval Europe. Papermaking spread west.

colonisation.value: Not a coloniser in the modern sense. It ruled a vast inherited empire that fragmented after a succession plan (802) and civil war (809).

riseSignals.value: A revolution starting in Khurasan (750) that drew on discontent with the Umayyads, especially among non-Arab Muslims. A new capital, Baghdad, at the centre of trade.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Abbasid Caliphate (checked 5 Nov 2026); Britannica: Abbasid caliphate (checked 8 Nov 2026)

peakPeriod.value: The reign of Harun al-Rashid (786–809), traditionally the height of Abbasid power and prestige.

declineSignals.value: Civil war after Harun, the cost and power of the slave army, provincial breakaways, falling tax revenue, and takeover by Buyid and Seljuk warlords.

outcome.value: Conquest. The Mongols under Hulagu sacked Baghdad in 1258 and executed the caliph. A symbolic Abbasid caliphate continued in Cairo under the Mamluks (1261–1517) until the Ottoman conquest.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Abbasid Caliphate (checked 5 Nov 2026); Britannica: Abbasid caliphate (checked 8 Nov 2026)

sources.value: Arabic chronicles (al-Tabari), scholarly works, coins, and Byzantine and Chinese sources. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Kennedy (2016).

overallCertainty.value: Good for politics and culture. Population figures are lacking. Some dates (e.g. the Mustansiriya madrasa, 1227 or 1234) and numbers vary between sources. Britannica (checked 8 Nov 2026) agrees on 750–1258, the first caliph al-Saffah, the move to Baghdad and the fall in the Mongol siege of 1258; it places the high point more broadly, from 750 to 833 (al-Mansur, Harun al-Rashid, al-Maʾmun).
overallCertainty.source: Wikipedia: Abbasid Caliphate (checked 5 Nov 2026); Britannica: Abbasid caliphate (checked 8 Nov 2026)
